strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem in latent diffusion training: how to use pretrained vision representations as more than an external alignment signal. The proposed REGLUE framework is technically coherent, combining VAE latents, compressed local VFM features, a global token, and REPA-style alignment within a SiT velocity objective.

Empirical evidence is strong on ImageNet 256x256. The method improves SiT-B/2 FID from 33.0 to 12.9 at 400K steps, outperforms REPA, ReDi, and REG under matched settings, and scales favorably to SiT-XL/2, reaching 2.5 FID without CFG at 1M steps and 1.53 FID with CFG at 160 epochs.

The ablation study is unusually thorough. Table 1 separates local vs global semantics, linear vs nonlinear compression, multi-layer features, and alignment; additional experiments study compressor width, channel count, VFM choice, semantic preservation via probing/segmentation, unconditional generation, CFG, and limited-data regimes.

The central design choice, a nonlinear spatial semantic compressor, is well motivated and supported. The paper gives evidence that it preserves more semantic information than PCA and that this preservation correlates with better generative performance.

The method is practical in the sense that it keeps the SiT token sequence essentially unchanged for local features by channel-wise fusion, adds only a small parameter increase, and does not require a VFM at sampling time.
weaknesses: The contribution is mostly an effective composition and refinement of very recent ideas rather than a fundamentally new generative modeling principle. It builds directly on REPA, ReDi, and REG, and the conceptual novelty is concentrated in nonlinear multi-layer local compression plus unified local/global joint modeling.

The experimental scope is narrow for the strength of some claims: nearly all main results are on ImageNet 256x256 with SiT backbones. There are no 512x512 results, no text-to-image or more open-ended generation setting, and no broader dataset suite beyond limited-data ImageNet and auxiliary probing/segmentation analyses.

Compute and fairness details could be clearer. Parameter counts appear to exclude the compressor and VFM feature extraction/precomputation pipeline, and training-time overhead from VFM feature extraction, storage, compressor training, and extra prediction heads is not fully quantified against baselines.

Some comparisons to long-trained state-of-the-art models are favorable but not decisive: with CFG, REGLUE improves over REG at matched 80/160 epochs, but the best reported REG/REPA results at 800 epochs still have lower FID. The paper’s strongest claim is accelerated convergence rather than absolute state of the art.

Reproducibility is incomplete as presented. The abstract says code is available, but the manuscript shows a blank code URL, and several implementation choices that may affect results, such as loss weights, feature normalization, cached feature handling, and exact baseline reproduction settings, would need released code for confidence.

The method introduces extra design complexity and hyperparameters, including compressor architecture, selected VFM layers, compression dimension, local/global loss weights, and alignment layer. The ablations are helpful, but sensitivity across datasets, backbones, and resolutions remains uncertain.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: improving latent diffusion training by incorporating semantic representations from vision foundation models. The idea of jointly modeling VAE latents with compact local VFM features and a global token is well aligned with recent REPA/ReDi/REG-style work.

The empirical ImageNet 256x256 results are reasonably strong. REGLUE improves FID over SiT-B/2, REPA, ReDi, and REG under the reported settings, and the larger SiT-XL/2 experiments suggest faster convergence than several baselines.

The ablation coverage is useful. The manuscript studies local vs. global semantics, nonlinear vs. PCA compression, multi-layer feature aggregation, compressor channel count/capacity, different VFMs, unconditional generation, CFG settings, and limited-data training.

The semantic compressor is simple and practical: a shallow convolutional autoencoder that preserves spatial structure while reducing the VFM feature dimensionality. The probing/segmentation analyses provide some supporting evidence that the compressed features retain meaningful semantics.
weaknesses: The contribution is quite incremental relative to REPA, ReDi, and REG. The method largely combines known ingredients: REPA-style alignment, ReDi-style joint modeling of patch features, REG-style global token modeling, and a learned nonlinear compressor. The paper does not make a compelling case that the conceptual advance is substantial rather than an engineering combination of recent methods.

The experimental scope is narrow for the strength of the claims. Almost all core evidence is on ImageNet 256x256 with SiT backbones and FID-based evaluation. There are no higher-resolution results, no text-conditioned generation, no transfer to other datasets/domains, and no demonstration that the approach generalizes beyond this benchmark setup.

Compute and efficiency claims are under-specified. The paper emphasizes unchanged or negligible inference-time cost, but REGLUE samples additional semantic/global variables, adds projection and prediction heads, requires VFM feature extraction/precomputation, and trains an offline compressor. Wall-clock training cost, storage overhead, preprocessing cost, and sampling throughput are not reported against REG/ReDi/REPA.

Fairness of comparisons is not fully convincing. Parameter counts appear to exclude the compressor/VFM pipeline and possibly auxiliary preprocessing costs. It is also unclear which baselines are re-run under identical code, VFM features, training budgets, sampler settings, and evaluation protocols versus copied from prior work.

The strongest FID gains without CFG are notable, but the state-of-the-art CFG comparison is more modest: REGLUE improves over REG at matched 80/160 epochs, but does not surpass longer-trained REG/REPA. This weakens the broader claim that the method is a major advance in image generation quality.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says code is available but the manuscript leaves the URL blank. Several implementation details that may materially affect results, such as exact feature caching, normalization, conditioning/dropout for CFG over semantic variables, compressor data split, and memory/storage requirements, are not sufficiently specified.

The paper lacks uncertainty estimates or repeated runs. Given that many comparisons are small at the stronger-model scale, e.g. FID 3.4 vs. 3.2 or 2.7 vs. 2.5, the absence of variance or confidence intervals makes it hard to judge whether some gains are robust.

Some claims are overstated. Statements such as keeping inference-time compute essentially unchanged and unlocking full nonlinear spatial semantics are stronger than what the experiments directly establish. The evidence supports useful improvement on a specific benchmark, but not such broad conclusions.

Limitations and societal impact discussion are thin. The limitations focus mostly on compute constraints and future scaling, with little discussion of generative-model risks, dataset bias, misuse, or whether using stronger VFMs changes bias propagation in the generated samples.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem in latent diffusion training: how to exploit pretrained vision foundation model representations beyond external alignment or narrow global/local signals. The proposed REGLUE framework is technically coherent, combining VAE latents, compressed patch-level VFM semantics, a global CLS token, and REPA-style alignment in one SiT objective.

The empirical evidence is strong for an Algorithms/General contribution. The paper reports consistent gains on ImageNet 256x256 across SiT-B/2 and SiT-XL/2, conditional and unconditional settings, with and without classifier-free guidance. The convergence improvements are particularly compelling: REGLUE reaches or exceeds several prior methods with fewer training iterations.

The ablation study is unusually thorough. Table 1 separates local versus global modeling, linear versus nonlinear compression, multi-layer aggregation, and external alignment; later ablations examine compressor dimension, capacity, VFM layer choice, auxiliary compressor losses, different VFMs, CFG settings, and limited-data regimes.

The semantic compressor is a simple but effective design choice. The probing and segmentation analyses support the central claim that learned nonlinear compression preserves more useful semantics than PCA and that this correlates with generation quality.

The method appears practically attractive: the inference-time diffusion backbone has only a small parameter increase relative to the SiT baseline, and the authors make a reasonable case that the expensive semantic machinery is mainly a training-time aid.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate rather than high. REGLUE is largely a well-executed synthesis of recent ideas from REPA, ReDi, and REG, with the main new component being a learned convolutional compressor and the systematic global-local combination. This is valuable, but the paper should be careful not to overstate the novelty of joint feature modeling itself.

The evaluation is concentrated on ImageNet 256x256. This is a standard benchmark, but the claims about general generative modeling would be stronger with higher-resolution ImageNet, another natural-image dataset, or a text-conditioned setting. The limitations section acknowledges this, but the current evidence leaves open whether the approach scales beyond this relatively controlled setup.

The practical compute accounting is incomplete. The paper reports model parameters and training iterations, but the method requires VFM feature extraction, offline compressor training, storage or recomputation of semantic targets, and additional velocity/alignment losses during training. Wall-clock time, memory, and feature-storage costs relative to REPA/ReDi/REG would make the efficiency claims more convincing.

Some comparisons could be better normalized. The paper compares against strong baselines, but not all methods are matched for total compute, auxiliary feature extraction cost, VFM choice, or training duration. The DINOv3 result is clearly marked, which is good, but the broader efficiency story would benefit from a more explicit apples-to-apples compute table.

Reproducibility details are mostly present, but the manuscript states that code is available at an empty placeholder. Given the number of interacting implementation choices, public code or a complete release plan is important for confidence.

The method depends on the quality and type of the frozen VFM. Results with CLIP-L are notably worse than with DINO variants, suggesting the approach may be sensitive to representation choice. This is explored briefly but not deeply explained.

strengths: The paper presents a clear Algorithms/General contribution: jointly modeling VAE latents, compact local VFM semantics, and a global VFM token inside a SiT diffusion backbone. The motivation is well connected to recent REPA, ReDi, and REG lines of work.

Empirical results are strong on ImageNet 256x256. REGLUE improves FID over SiT-B/2, REPA, ReDi, and REG at comparable training budgets, and the XL-scale results show faster convergence and competitive CFG performance against longer-trained representation-guided diffusion models.

The ablation study is unusually thorough: local vs global semantics, linear vs nonlinear compression, multi-layer features, alignment losses, compressor dimensionality/capacity, VFM choice, fusion strategy, compute/FLOPs, and additional metrics are all examined.

The semantic compressor is simple and practical. Channel-wise fusion preserves inference token count, and the paper reports negligible parameter/throughput overhead relative to REG while improving quality.
The manuscript is generally readable and well structured, with a useful limitations section acknowledging incomplete ultra-long training and high-resolution scaling.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate rather than high: the method is largely a well-engineered combination of existing ideas from REPA, ReDi, and REG, with the main new component being a learned convolutional compressor replacing PCA. The gains are convincing, but the algorithmic leap is incremental.

The main evidence is concentrated on ImageNet generation. Food-101 and ImageNet-512 results are brief and only reported for SiT-B/2; there is limited evidence that the approach generalizes to more diverse datasets, text-conditioned generation, video, or downstream controllability settings.

Fairness/reproducibility concerns remain. The abstract says code is available but the link is blank, no variance over seeds is reported, and many comparisons depend on training budget, epochs, CFG settings, or baselines from recent/preprint works. Stronger reproducibility details and confidence intervals would make the case more robust.

The method depends on frozen VFMs and precomputed semantic features, but the practical storage/preprocessing cost and wall-clock pipeline complexity are not discussed as fully as inference throughput. Training-time overhead is addressed partially via PFLOPs, but operational costs may still matter.

Some claims about semantic preservation and 'diffusability' are plausible but not fully causal. The probing, segmentation, and frequency analyses support the compressor design, yet they do not isolate all confounders between representation quality, dimensionality, frequency content, and generative performance.

The paper does not fully explore whether REGLUE still helps at full convergence. The authors note resource constraints and stop XL experiments at 1M iterations, so it remains unclear how much of the benefit is acceleration versus asymptotic quality improvement.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: improving latent diffusion training by injecting semantic representations from vision foundation models, which is relevant to current computer vision generative modeling.

The proposed REGLUE framework is technically coherent: it jointly models VAE latents, compressed patch-level VFM features, and a global CLS token within a SiT backbone, with an additional REPA-style alignment loss.

The empirical results on ImageNet 256x256 are strong. The paper reports consistent FID improvements over SiT, REPA, ReDi, and REG at both B/2 and XL/2 scales, including faster convergence under comparable iteration budgets.

The ablation study is fairly extensive. The paper separately analyzes local vs global semantics, nonlinear vs PCA compression, multi-layer VFM features, alignment losses, compression dimensionality, compressor capacity, VFM choice, fusion strategy, CFG settings, and some transfer to Food-101/ImageNet-512.

The semantic compressor is a plausible and useful component. The probing, segmentation, and frequency-profile diagnostics support the claim that nonlinear compression preserves more semantic information than PCA while producing representations that are easier for diffusion to model.
The paper discusses limitations around long training schedules and high-resolution scaling, and includes compute/throughput measurements rather than reporting only final FID.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental. REGLUE largely combines ideas already present in REPA, ReDi, and REG: VFM alignment, joint image-feature diffusion, and global semantic token modeling. The main new ingredient is a learned convolutional compressor plus a particular combination of these components, which is useful but not a conceptually large advance.

The paper’s strongest claims rely heavily on FID improvements, often under narrow ImageNet-centered settings. Although additional metrics are included in the supplement, the main scientific case would be stronger with broader datasets, more resolutions, and more diverse generation settings beyond ImageNet-style class-conditional synthesis.

The fairness of compute accounting remains somewhat unclear. The method depends on extracting VFM features and training a compressor offline; while the paper reports some PFLOPs and throughput, the practical cost of feature precomputation, storage, and pipeline complexity is not fully characterized.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing or incomplete release information: the abstract says code is available but no actual link is provided in the extracted manuscript. The paper also does not report variance over seeds, confidence intervals, or robustness of the gains to implementation details.

Some comparisons to state of the art are not fully satisfying. With classifier-free guidance, REGLUE improves over shorter-trained REG but does not clearly surpass the best longer-trained VFM-based models; the contribution is therefore more about convergence efficiency than absolute state of the art, and this distinction should be made more modestly.

Several design choices appear empirically tuned without deep justification, including the loss weights, alignment block choice, compression channel count, selected VFM layers, and the additive channel-wise fusion of projected latent and semantic tokens. The ablations help, but the method still feels like a carefully optimized recipe rather than a principled framework.

The presentation occasionally overclaims. Phrases such as “unified” and “synergistically” are stronger than what the evidence establishes; many gains come from local compressed features, while the global token and external alignment provide relatively small additional improvements in the final configuration.

The societal impact, failure modes, and risks of improving high-fidelity image generation are not meaningfully discussed. For a generative model paper, issues such as misuse, bias inherited from ImageNet/VFMs, memorization, and synthetic media risks deserve more attention.

strengths: The paper makes a clear Algorithms/General contribution: REGLUE extends recent VFM-guided diffusion work by jointly modeling VAE latents, local patch-level VFM semantics, and a global CLS token, with a lightweight nonlinear semantic compressor. This is a natural but useful synthesis of REPA/ReDi/REG-style ideas.

The empirical evidence is strong on ImageNet 256x256. The reported gains are consistent across SiT-B/2 and SiT-XL/2, conditional and unconditional generation, with and without classifier-free guidance. The improvements over REPA, ReDi, and REG are meaningful, especially in convergence speed and FID at matched or near-matched compute.

The ablation study is unusually thorough. The paper isolates local vs global semantics, linear PCA vs nonlinear compression, multilayer features, external alignment, compression dimensionality, compressor capacity, VFM choice, fusion strategy, resampling, CFG settings, and limited-data behavior.

The semantic compressor is well motivated and supported by both downstream semantic preservation probes and a frequency/diffusability diagnostic. These analyses make the main design choice more convincing than a pure benchmark-driven claim.
The method keeps inference-time architecture and throughput essentially comparable to REG by channel-wise fusion rather than sequence concatenation, which strengthens the practical case.

The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and gives enough implementation detail in the supplement to support reproducibility, including optimizer settings, compressor architecture, sampling setup, and compute comparisons.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate rather than high. The method combines known ingredients: VFM representation alignment, joint image-feature diffusion, global token modeling, and learned compression. The nonlinear spatial compressor is useful, but the paper is closer to a strong engineering and empirical consolidation than a fundamentally new generative modeling paradigm.

The main evidence remains concentrated on ImageNet-style generation. Supplementary Food-101 and ImageNet-512 results help, but the broader generality to text-to-image, more diverse datasets, downstream controllability, or non-object-centric domains is not established.

Several comparisons depend on training-budget and protocol choices that are favorable but not fully exhaustive. The authors acknowledge that SiT-XL/2+REGLUE is not trained to ultra-long schedules, so it is unclear whether the relative advantage persists at full convergence against all strong baselines.

The paper reports many single-run FID numbers without variance or confidence intervals. Given that some final gains over REG at larger scale are modest, run-to-run stability would strengthen the acceptance case.

The method relies on an offline VFM feature extraction and compressor training pipeline. Although compute is accounted for in one table and the compressor is lightweight, the total system complexity and storage/precomputation costs are more involved than vanilla SiT and deserve a clearer practical discussion in the main paper.

The abstract says code is available but the extracted manuscript appears to omit the actual URL. This is minor if fixed, but currently weakens the reproducibility claim. The societal-impact discussion is also minimal for a generative image model.
